messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Weiss is a 68-year-old psychologist who has been married for decades, and it is still difficult for him to speak plainly about the relationship in which he was assaulted by a romantic partner. What he can describe comes in fragments. He remembers the bicycle first: it had been knocked sideways in the hallway outside the apartment after an argument, the front wheel still slowly turning while she stood over him in clothes he now cannot bring himself to wear anything resembling. He can call up sharp visual stills—the angle of the wheel, the fabric at her wrist, the cramped entryway—but not a continuous account of how one moment became the next. At other times there is no image at all, only a sudden wash of the same dread and humiliation. Those broken, photographic pieces have left him feeling that his old assumptions about intimacy, safety, and even his own judgment were destroyed; if he could be trapped and hurt in what he thought was a loving relationship, then people are not what they seem, and something in him must be fundamentally inadequate for having missed it.

In the months after he left that relationship, the world began to organize itself around reminders. Passing a bicycle chained outside his office building could stop him short. Riding public transportation, especially when pressed in among strangers, brought back the trapped feeling of that apartment hallway. What unsettled him most, and what he is ashamed to admit, is being alone with women in enclosed spaces. In his work as a psychologist, this has become painfully concrete: he notices his body tense when a female patient is the last appointment of the day and the waiting room has emptied out. In those moments the trigger does not remain a simple reminder. It lands immediately on the conclusions he has already drawn—people can turn dangerous without warning, he cannot trust his own reading of them, he may not be able to protect himself—and the reminder feels like proof that the world is still unsafe.

Because he has come to believe both that others are deceptive and that he himself is not equal to managing what happened, Martin works hard to keep tight control over his internal life. He never allows himself to feel or express anger, especially toward women, as if letting himself register it would make him lose control or reveal something ugly about him. He monitors his face and voice in sessions, keeps his feelings flattened, and avoids wearing clothes that resemble what he had on during the assault. When a bicycle appears unexpectedly on the street, or he finds himself hemmed in by a crowd, he becomes even more deliberate about containing himself, gripping hard to composure and pushing down whatever rises in him.

That effort has not made him feel safer. If anything, Martin has become preoccupied with danger. He watches other people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning changes in expression, stance, tone, and proximity. Crowded places are especially difficult because there are too many people to track; being alone with a woman can feel intolerably exposing because all of his attention narrows onto whether he is missing some threat. Nights are worse. He wakes and checks whether he is safe, listening to the house, looking toward the bedroom door, more alert after dark than during the day. The more he lives in this state of vigilance, the more convinced he becomes that his earlier beliefs were naive, that danger hides in ordinary encounters, and that his sensitivity is necessary because he cannot rely on anyone being what they seem.

This vigilance also seems to pull the trauma closer. When Martin lies awake at night scanning for danger, the memory returns not as a narrative but as isolated images, or else as raw emotional force without a picture. Watching others so closely during the day leaves him primed for the same flashes: a bicycle wheel, a woman’s sleeve, the crush of bodies in a crowded train. And because he keeps cutting off anger and clamping down on feeling, he never gets beyond those frozen moments. He cannot assemble a coherent story even for himself. The event remains a set of alarming fragments, which only strengthens his sense that the world no longer follows understandable rules.

Over time his habits have narrowed his life. He structures his practice to reduce situations in which he might be alone with women, lingers with his office door open between sessions, and avoids busy professional meetings when he can. Avoiding certain clothes, certain routes, certain kinds of contact has made the triggers more potent rather than less; bicycles stand out immediately, crowded rooms feel more charged, and female presence is noticed before anything else. His wife has seen how little sleep he gets and how much effort it takes for him to get through a workday that once felt natural. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was beginning to organize even his clinical work around fear. He says he wants, at minimum, to be able to sit with a patient or walk past a bicycle rack without feeling that his whole body has to brace for harm, but what frightens him most is the possibility that this is what his life has become: permanently watchful, emotionally constricted, and unable to trust either other people or his own mind.
